tone_statements.quote: The tonal system of Mushere basically comprises three levels i e high H d y mid M a y and low L a … In addition to the three basic tone levels mentioned above low mid high which correspond to the three musical notes DO MI and SOL a fourth tone level i e half low placed between mid and low is of phonological re levance in the language … As there is a phonemic tone level between low and mid cf 2 3 there is another intermediate tone level between high and mid i e half high haH Thus the language makes use of the complete musical scale comprising all five notes between DO and SOL

sources.note: Nothing. Purely tonal account: sec. 2 (p.299) 'The tonal system of Mushere basically comprises three levels i.e. high, mid and low', plus a phonemic half-low (2.3, p.299-301) and half-high (2.5, p.305) level = five level tones; seven tonal verb classes, tonal aspect stems, tonal locative case. The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the article.

tone.quote: The tonal system of Mushere basically comprises three levels i e high H d y mid M a y and low L a … In addition to the three basic tone levels mentioned above low mid high which correspond to the three musical notes DO MI and SOL a fourth tone level i e half low placed between mid and low is of phonological re levance in the language … As there is a phonemic tone level between low and mid cf 2 3 there is another intermediate tone level between high and mid i e half high haH Thus the language makes use of the complete musical scale comprising all five notes between DO and SOL
tone.says: Five level tones: basic high, mid, low plus a phonemic half-low (downstepped mid or raised low, lexical in some nouns) and a tentative half-high marking locative on high-tone nouns; aspect is tonal.

sources.citation: Shadrach, Nanzhwan Caleb. n.d. An Introduction to the Chakfem Language (Reading and Writing in the Chakfem Language). 24 pp. typescript posted by Roger Blench as 'Chakfem grammar sketch' (= Glottolog hh ref 143873).
sources.note: Nothing on word stress. p.1: 'Chakfem is a tonal language, which means that one word, more often than not, means more than one thing depending on the tone'; p.4-5 'three basic tonal notes.. low tone, middle tone, and high tone' with an orthography using 'tonal consonants'. 'Stressed verbs' on p.21 = emphatic reduplicated verb forms, not prosodic stress.

sources.quote: On the other hand, various forms in specific individual languages present a nearly isolating profile with frequent use of grammatical tone, such as in the following examples from East Chadic Lele (ex. 26), Masa Chadic Musey (ex. 27), Central Chadic Mbara (ex. 28) and West Chadic Mushere (ex. 29): ... (29) Mushere (Jungraithmayr & Diyakal 2008 cit. in Schuh 2017: 165) ka náa ... ‘you have seen’ ká naá ... ‘you will see’ ... sources.note: Secondhand mention only. p.15 names Mushere among Chadic languages with a 'nearly isolating profile with frequent use of grammatical tone', ex. 29 ka náa 'you have seen' vs ká naá 'you will see' (J&D 2008 via Schuh 2017:165); pp.22-23 ex. 45 tabulates three STAMP (subject+TAM) series prog/pst/fut from J&D 2013:304 in which pst and fut differ by tone alone (1sg a vs á, 2m ka vs ká, 2f yi vs yí). No tone inventory, nothing on the five-level system; not a description of Mushere tonology.
